title: Calming the Storm
lead: Jesus’ presence brings hope even when it seems the boat is going down.
questions: Which storm in my life makes me suspect God of not caring, and does my fear run toward Him or away from Him?
Is my present storm really proof that I’m on the wrong course, or is it just the weather on the right one?
Whom have I criticized for weak faith in the middle of a storm instead of helping first, and how can I make it right?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: The new section of our journey is titled “There Is Hope When the Boat Is Sinking, the Bread Runs Out and the Tomb Is Sealed”: three of humanity’s oldest fears. The first story begins with the sentence “Let us cross to the other side.” It is Jesus who proposes this crossing; the storm will hit people sailing exactly where He led them. Jesus’ presence in the boat is not a guarantee of good weather. It is a guarantee of reaching the other side.

We even know what the boat looked like: a fishing vessel from that era has been recovered from the lake mud, eight meters long, sides waist-high, with a draft so shallow that in high waves it easily took on water. And the lake itself is shallow water in a deep bowl: no more than forty-four meters deep, ringed by hills four hundred meters high, from which cold air pours down through the ravines and in a quarter of an hour turns a glassy surface into a cauldron. The professionals in the crew knew the diagnosis: a shell with water inside it is no longer sailing; it is sinking. Meanwhile, in the stern, on the helmsman’s cushion, Jesus is asleep, exhausted after a whole day of teaching. The one who sleeps is the one who knows whose hands the boat is in.

The disciples wake Him with a sentence the Gospel could have smoothed over, but didn’t: “Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?” It is a complaint, not a textbook prayer, and yet it was heard; what counted was the direction they ran while they were shouting. Jesus stands up and speaks to the elements as to an enraged animal, literally: be quiet, be muzzled. No formula, no request to the Father, just a command in His own name. And “it was perfectly calm.” But now the disciples are more afraid than they were in the storm: “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?” The question is left unanswered on purpose, because the answer had long stood in the psalm about sailors: it is the LORD who “calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Psalm 107:29). This time the command didn’t come down from heaven. It came from the mouth of Someone who had been asleep on their cushion.

A storm is not proof that you’ve gone off course; sometimes the worst weather meets people sailing exactly according to His instructions. And Jesus first calmed the storm, and only then asked about faith. That is the order: rescue first, then the conversation. And Jesus’ sleep in the stern says one more thing: a boat in which He is sleeping cannot sink.

Today we begin a new section of our journey: “There Is Hope When the Boat Is Sinking, the Bread Runs Out and the Tomb Is Sealed.” Three of humanity’s oldest fears, three stories in which Jesus stands face to face with the elements, with want, and with death. We begin with the elements, and not figuratively. The first scene of this section takes place at night, on the water, in a boat that is really starting to sink. And it begins with a sentence that is easy to miss: “Let us cross to the other side.” It is Jesus who proposes this crossing. The storm about to break will hit people sailing exactly where He led them. It’s worth saying at the threshold of this whole section: Jesus’ presence in the boat is not a guarantee of good weather. It is a guarantee of reaching the other side.

sections.heading: Just as He Was
paragraphs: Mark adds details that carry the scent of an eyewitness account, which is no surprise, since Peter’s memory stands behind his Gospel. The disciples took Jesus with them “even as he was” (WEB), with no preparations, straight from the boat He had been using all day to teach the crowds about seed and soil. Other boats sailed with them too, and after that not another word is said about them; a detail like that serves no purpose, so no one would have made it up. We even know what their vessel looked like: a fishing boat from that era has been recovered from the mud along the lakeshore, eight meters (about 27 feet) long, a little over two meters wide, its sides waist-high. Room for a dozen or so people and not one more. The key feature of these boats was their shallow draft: they were easy to pull up onto the beach and easy to haul full nets into, but in high waves they took on water just as easily. The Gospel isn’t telling a story about a ship. It’s telling a story about a nutshell.

sections.heading: A Lake in a Bowl
paragraphs: People unfamiliar with this body of water sometimes wonder how professional fishermen could be caught off guard by the weather. Just look at the numbers. The Sea of Galilee is twenty-one kilometers (thirteen miles) long and no more than forty-four meters (about 150 feet) deep, and it is surrounded by hills that rise four to five hundred meters above the surface. Shallow water in a deep bowl: cold mountain air pours down the ravines between the slopes onto the warm surface and in a quarter of an hour turns smooth water into a cauldron. You can’t see a storm like that coming from far off, and you can’t wait it out near the shore, because it doesn’t roll in; it explodes. Mark writes that “a violent windstorm came up,” that the waves were breaking over the side and the boat was filling with water. That is a diagnosis the four fishermen in the crew could make with professional precision: past a certain point, a shell with water inside it is no longer sailing; it is sinking. The experience that had told them all their lives how things were was now telling them this was the end.

sections.heading: Asleep in the Stern
paragraphs: At that very moment, in the stern, on the helmsman’s cushion, Jesus is asleep. This is the only place in the Gospels where we see Him sleeping, and it’s hard to imagine more telling circumstances: He sleeps through a gale that terrifies the professionals. This sleep has two layers. The first is simply human: Jesus has been teaching all day and is so tired that neither wind nor water wakes Him. We saw Him weary at the well; today we see Him exhausted on a cushion. The incarnation means that too. The second layer goes deeper. The psalmist wrote: “I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8). Sleeping in a storm is not numbness but the deepest form of trust: the one who sleeps is the one who knows whose hands the boat is in. In the same boat, in the same storm, some are dying of fear and One is asleep. The difference isn’t in the weather. It’s in what each one knows about the Father.

sections.heading: Don’t You Care?
paragraphs: The disciples wake Him with a sentence the Gospel had every right to smooth over, and yet it left it as it was: “Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?” This is not a textbook prayer. It is a complaint, a reproach, the cry of people standing ankle-deep in water who, for a split second, suspect God of indifference. If Mark kept it, then we have a right to prayers like that too. God doesn’t require the drowning to use correct phrasing; He accepts a cry in whatever state the one crying is in. And look at what matters most in their shout: they woke Him. With all their complaint and all their fear, they still ran to the stern, not to the oars. Faith in a crisis rarely sounds beautiful. Sometimes its entire content is the direction a person runs while shouting.

sections.heading: “Silence! Be Still!”
paragraphs: What follows, Mark describes in words that send a chill down the spine. Jesus gets up and rebukes the wind, and to the lake He speaks as to an enraged animal: literally, be quiet, be muzzled. In Mark, “rebuked” is the same word Jesus used a little earlier to silence and cast out demons; to the wind and to the darkness He speaks in the same tone of authority. There is no prayer formula here, no request to the Father, no incantation. There is a command given to the elements in His own name, and the elements obey at once: the wind drops, and not even a swell is left behind, only “perfectly calm.” The ancients sensed well what had happened here. Religion asks and offers sacrifices; someone who gives orders to the forces of nature and is obeyed displays an authority of an entirely different order. And Israel knew even more. In its Scriptures, rebuking the sea is an action reserved for one Subject alone: “For He spoke and raised a tempest that lifted the waves of the sea. … Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He brought them out of their distress. He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Psalm 107:25, 28–29). The psalm about sailors who cried out to the LORD, and He turned their storm into calm, had just played out before their eyes to the letter. Except that the command didn’t come down from heaven. It came from the mouth of Someone who, a minute earlier, had been asleep on their cushion.

sections.heading: Who Is This?
paragraphs: And here Mark records something psychologically astonishing: after the storm is stilled, the disciples are more afraid than they were during it. “Overwhelmed with fear, they asked one another, ‘Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?’” The storm they understood; dangerous, but familiar. What they can’t get their heads around is the calm. Because if Someone is sailing in their boat whose orders the lake carries out, then every category they have used to describe Him until now has just gone under. Their question is left unanswered in the text, and that is deliberate: the answer had long stood in a psalm every one of them knew. Who is He? The One who alone calms the seas. Mark doesn’t spell it out, because he wants the reader to finish the sentence, and that question is, at bottom, addressed to us. Even before their fear grew into that question, Jesus had asked them His own: “Why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith?” He isn’t scolding them for being afraid of the storm; fear in a storm is human. He is asking why their fear was alone, without faith, when they were sailing with Him and He had said: to the other side. He hadn’t promised a calm voyage. He had promised the far shore.

It’s also worth asking what the crossing was for in the first place. The answer waits in the first sentence of the next chapter: on the other side lay “the region of the Gerasenes,” pagan territory, with herds of pigs on the hillsides, and on the shore a man was waiting whom no one tried to save anymore, living among the tombs, written off by everyone. This whole night-long battle with the elements took place on the way to one desperate man on the wrong side of the lake. The storm struck a boat that was going to the rescue. That belongs to the picture too: resistance that erupts halfway across is often the best proof that the crossing is worth finishing.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: This story sets the tone for the whole section we begin today, and it sets something in us as well. First: a storm is not proof that you’ve gone off course. The disciples sailed into a gale while following His instructions exactly; sometimes the worst weather meets people on the right course. Second: you are allowed to pray the way you can at that moment. The prayer “Don’t You care that we are perishing?” was answered, even though theologically it was limping on both legs; what counted was the direction they ran. Third: you recognize Jesus’ presence in your boat not by the absence of storms but by the fact that the storm doesn’t get the last word. “Let us cross to the other side” was a sentence with a promise inside it; they just didn’t hear it until afterward. And Jesus’ sleep in the stern said the same thing without words: a boat in which He is sleeping cannot sink. And one word to us as a community: we are all in one boat, and sailing with us are people for whom the water is already very high. Before we point out to someone that their faith is shouting instead of trusting, let’s remember that Jesus first calmed the storm and only then asked about faith. That is the order: rescue first, then the conversation.
